The AEAD system in JET comprises two arrays of four toroidally spaced antennas (eight in total) that can excite a spectrum of toroidal mode numbers up to n ≤ 20.
The probability of resonance detection decreases as the plasma-antenna separation increases, from ~62% for separations around 15 cm to ~38% for separations around 10 cm or more.

The measured damping rate of the low-frequency AE mode increased with increasing plasma-antenna separation, from |γ/ω0| ≈ 0.2% at 15 cm to |γ/ω0| ≈ 1.2% at 10 cm, while the high-frequency mode had a consistent damping rate of |γ/ω0| ≈ 0.4%.
The computational modeling using CASTOR indicated that the high-frequency mode was an n=0 Global Alfvén Eigenmode (GAE) and the low-frequency mode was likely an n=2 Toroidal Alfvén Eigenmode (TAE).
In the transition from limiter to X-point configuration, the high-frequency AE mode was detected throughout, but its damping rate increased, while the low-frequency mode became unidentifiable.
The computational results showed that the antenna-driven mode energy decreased with increasing plasma-antenna separation, but the mode damping rate did not change for a given magnetic configuration.
The studied discharges had a toroidal magnetic field of 3 T, plasma current of 1.7 MA, central electron density of ~3.8x10^19 m^-3, and central electron temperature of ~1.5 keV.

Decreasing the plasma-antenna separation from ~15 cm to ~10 cm improved the plasma-antenna coupling and AE excitation, but also increased the distance between the antenna and some magnetic probes, potentially making AE detection more difficult.
The computational modeling in CASTOR included up to 7 poloidal harmonics for the plasma and 9 vacuum harmonics, with a normalized resistivity of ηˆ = 1.6x10^-9.
The CASTOR code modeled an external antenna in the vacuum region between the plasma and the wall, and scanned the antenna frequency to diagnose the plasma response for a given toroidal mode number.
The probability of resonance detection was higher in limiter configuration (62%) compared to X-point configuration (38%), suggesting reduced plasma-antenna coupling in the X-point configuration.
The transition from limiter to X-point configuration was found to increase the damping rate of AEs by approximately threefold in previous JET studies.

Inspired by JET experiments, two poloidally separated antennas were installed at one toroidal location in Alcator C-Mod to actively probe stable AEs, with lower damping rates measured in X-point compared to limiter configuration.
The computational work by Dvornova et al. accurately modeled the plasma-antenna coupling and explained some of the experimental observations, motivating the current study.
The CASTOR code was recently updated by the authors to allow the toroidal mode number n=0, which caused divergences in previous versions.
